title: Label Propagation
description: Nodes never merge; they only change labels, by a weighted vote of their neighbours’ labels. Asynchronous versus synchronous updates, visiting order, ties, confirming stability, and cycles.
hook: Nobody draws the circles. So where do they come from?
cardText: Each node looks at its neighbours’ current labels and joins the group it is most strongly connected to. Names stay, labels change; it may settle, or it may swing back and forth.
prerequisitesText: [Foundations](../../foundations/index.html): graphs, edge weights, cut. The “merge” of Module 04 is replaced here by “relabel”.
nextText: Module 06 moves from local votes to spectral information about the whole graph.
review: The first three modules really put members together by merging. This module **merges no nodes at all**: each node only updates the label it carries, and a group is “the nodes with the same label”.

objectives.text: Tell a node’s name (identity, fixed) from its label (membership, changing), and explain why the algorithm needs no K.
Count weighted votes by label: C’s votes are B = 1 + 4 = 5, D = 2, E = 1. Weight is compared, not the number of neighbours.
Work through a full asynchronous round by hand, and explain why stability needs a round with zero changes (G01: 2 rounds).
Tell apart the three stopping states stable, cycle and limit; find a cycle under synchronous updates.
Explain how visiting order, tie rule and edge weights change the result and the round count (reverse order: 3 rounds; C–D = 10: cut 5).
Judge a result by its cut and name the limits (no K, no balance guarantee, depends on the rules); implement vote counting and the stopping test in Python.

problem.input: A weighted undirected graph, a visiting order, an update mode (async / sync), a tie rule (min / max / keep), and a maximum number of rounds.
problem.output: Each node’s final label, the groups by label, the votes at every step, the cut, the number of rounds and the stopping state.
problem.objective: Let tightly connected nodes gather under one label “by themselves”, without fixing the number of clusters in advance.
problem.constraints: Each update reads only that node’s neighbours; node names never change; the tie rule must be deterministic.
problem.assumptions: Edge weights are positive and mean connection strength; each node starts with its own name as its label; an isolated node keeps its label.
problem.stop: stable: a full round with zero changes; cycle: a label state repeats; limit: the maximum number of rounds is reached. Only stable may be called “converged”.

filmNote: Continues the story of the author’s original Lab05 film: from an address book to a chip, then the rule taken apart layer by layer. A slow walkthrough follows the two rounds on G01 vote by vote.
labNote: Update one node at a time or play whole rounds; switch async/sync, the tie rule and the visiting order, and change the weight of C–D. The panel on the right itemises the current vote; the log below records every step.
challengeTip: Challenge 4 asks you to find a setting that cycles on your own: try it in the lab first.

mistakes.title: Treating the label as the name
mistakes.why: A node’s name is its identity and never changes; what changes is the label C carries.
mistakes.counter: After round 1, C carries label B, but it is still node C, with the same edges and weights.
mistakes.fix: Say “C’s label becomes B”, and read groups as “nodes with the same label”.

mistakes.title: Counting neighbours instead of weight
mistakes.wrong: A has two neighbours with B and one with D, so B wins.
mistakes.why: A label’s votes are the sum of edge weights of the neighbours carrying it, not their number.
mistakes.counter: The tie graph from the original Lab05 repository: B and C carry B (1 each), D carries D (4). Weighted, B = 2 and D = 4, so A picks D.
mistakes.fix: Add up edge weights per label.

mistakes.title: Calling it converged because some nodes did not change
mistakes.wrong: B and E did not change in round 1, so they are stable.
mistakes.why: Once a later node changes, earlier nodes see different neighbour labels next time.
mistakes.counter: Three nodes change in round 1 on G01; only a full round 2 with zero changes confirms stable, for 2 rounds in total.
mistakes.fix: Use “a full round with zero changes” as the test for stable, and count that confirmation round.

mistakes.title: Calling a cycle “unfinished” or “converged”
mistakes.wrong: Synchronous updates still change at the round limit, so report stable or raise the limit.
mistakes.why: Synchronous updates read one old snapshot, so two nodes that support each other swap labels at the same time and keep returning to the same state.
mistakes.counter: Two nodes, synchronous: A↔B swap back and forth; G01 under synchronous updates also returns to round 1’s state in round 3 (period 2).
mistakes.fix: Detect repeated states and report cycle; compare against asynchronous updates or another tie rule.

mistakes.title: Comparing results by label names
mistakes.wrong: Forward order gives B/B/B/E/E and reverse order gives A/A/A/D/D, so the results differ.
mistakes.why: Label names are only markers; a grouping is about who is together.
mistakes.fix: Compare normalised groupings, not label strings.

limits:
- No K is given and group sizes are not balanced: one large group may swallow almost every node.
- The result depends on visiting order, update mode and tie rule; on the same graph, a different rule can change the number of rounds and even whether it stops.
- Synchronous updates can cycle; asynchronous updates stop on these examples, but the course does not claim they stop on every graph.
- The original paper (Raghavan, Albert, Kumara, 2007) stresses near-linear time: each round reads every edge a constant number of times. This course’s implementation follows that idea, scanning each node’s neighbours in turn.
- The 24-cell circuit and the contact graph are fictional teaching graphs; their numbers describe only those graphs.

pythonPackage.title: Implement vote counting and the stopping test
pythonPackage.md:
**Task** (`starter.py`):

1. `count_votes(adj, labels, vertex)`: add up neighbour edge weights by label.
2. The stopping test in the main loop: stable / cycle (limit is handled by the loop bound).

**Hint 1**: for neighbours with the same label, add their edge weights; C’s votes should be B = 5, D = 2, E = 1.

**Hint 2**: a full round with zero changes → stable; if the complete label state at the end of the round has appeared before → cycle. The checker also runs the author’s original 24-cell circuit and 28-person contact graph.

kept: The narrative “address book → chip → one local rule → taken apart layer by layer”, and the phrasing “a name is identity, a label is membership”.

Real node-by-node voting, async/sync, three tie rules, visiting order, editing the bridge weight, and the cycle counterexample; this module’s engine is adapted directly from the author’s `site/algorithm.js` (MIT).
The data of the 24-cell fictional circuit (geometric cut 88, LP cut 2) and the 28-person contact graph (3 rounds, cut 4).
The idea of a slow walkthrough of about a minute and a half: this module’s film comes with a slow vote-by-vote walkthrough.

references: Raghavan, U. N., Albert, R., & Kumara, S. (2007). Near linear time algorithm to detect community structures in large-scale networks. *Physical Review E*, 76, 036106.
